blocks.text: That the Prophets spoke of this animal may be the more probable because I learn from the Arabs something hitherto unknown, that the porcupine is an animal common in Syria. Damir, in the chapter دلدل [duldul] Duldul, or On the Porcupine: هو كثير ببلاد الشام والعراق وبلاد المغارب [huwa kathīr bi-bilād al-Shām wa-l-ʿIrāq wa-bilād al-Maghārib] It abounds in the region of Syria and Iraq (Mesopotamia and Babylonia), and [col. 1042] in the region of Megareb, that is, western Africa. He teaches the same about the hedgehog, thus: وهو صنفان قنفد يكون بارض مصر قدر الفار وقنفد يكون بارض الشام وعراق في قدر الكلب القلطي والفرق بينهما كالفرق بين الفار والجرذ [wa-huwa ṣinfān qunfud yakūn bi-arḍ Miṣr qadr al-fār wa-qunfud yakūn bi-arḍ al-Shām wa-ʿIrāq fī qadr al-kalb al-qalṭī wa-l-farq baynahumā ka-l-farq bayn al-fār wa-l-jurdh] The hedgehog is of two species. One is in the land of Egypt, of the size of a shrew; the other in the lands of Syria and Iraq (Mesopotamia and Babylonia), of the size of a Maltese dog, so that they differ as much as the shrew and the mouse differ. [II, 462] Those who infer that the kippod kippod קפוד is an aquatic animal from these words of Isaiah about Babylon, I will make it a possession of the kippod, and pools of water, do not even so adduce anything that stands in the way of our view. For among aquatic creatures too there is a species of hedgehog, which by Avicenna, Damir and Ibn al-Baitar is called قنفد بحري [qunfud baḥrī], by others ἐχῖνος θαλάσσιος [echinos thalassios], sea hedgehog, or else ποτάμιος [potamios], river hedgehog. For Paul of Aegina reported that there are also river hedgehogs. The Euphrates near Babylon could have teemed with them. At least we learn from Nearchus that hedgehogs of remarkable size are found near the islands lying off the mouth of the Euphrates. Strabo: Λέγει δὲ (ὁ Νέαρχος) ἐν ταῖς πρὸ τοῦ Εὐφράτου νήσοις φύεσθαι παγούρων καὶ ἐχίνων μεγέθη· [Legei de (ho Nearchos) en tais pro tou Euphratou nēsois phyesthai pagourōn kai echinōn megethē]. But we interpret the passage of Isaiah very differently, namely in this way: I will make it a possession of the kippod (that is, of the land hedgehog), even the pools of water. That is, not only will the city be laid waste, but the neighbouring pools too will dry up, so that they will be as fit a dwelling as the city for the land hedgehog, which delights above all in dry places. Thus in Sophon. II, 13. Nineveh is said to be made לשממה וציה, a desolation and dryness, and only then does it come about that the kippod lodges in it. And in Esa. XXXIV, 11., before Idumaea is handed over as a possession of the kippod, the streams are turned into pitch and the dust into brimstone.

To prove that the kippod kippod קפוד is a bird, it carries little weight that in Es. XXXIV, 11. it is named together with birds. For right in verse thirteen dragons and ostriches are joined together, although they are animals of entirely different kinds. And Zephaniah gathers flocks, beasts, the pelican and the kippod together into one bundle. This affects the reader all the more, since in a description of devastation the things that inspire horror are set forth in such a jumbled order. When Sophocles, in this line of the satyr play Amycus, mentions hares among many birds,
Γέρανοι, κορῶναι, γλαῦκες ἴκτινοι, λαγοὶ, [Geranoi, korōnai, glaukes iktinoi, lagoi,]

Cranes, crows, owls, kites, hares: who would conclude from this that the hare is a kind of bird? I know that someone has substituted λάροι [laroi], a kind of water bird, for λαγοὶ [lagoi]. But in vain. For Athenaeus, book 9, chapter 14, cites this line to prove that λαγοὶ [lagoi] is as much Attic as λαγώ [lagō]. So λαγοί [lagoi] must be retained. Conversely, in Lucian's Syrian Goddess you may see eagles named among many quadrupeds thus: Ἐν δὲ τῇ αὐλῇ ἄφετοι νέμονται βόες μεγάλοι, καὶ ἵπποι, καὶ αἐτοὶ, καὶ ἄρκτοι, καὶ λέοντες· [En de tē aulē aphetoi nemontai boes megaloi, kai hippoi, kai aetoi, kai arktoi, kai leontes] In the court, moreover, there graze freely great oxen, and horses, and eagles, and bears, and lions. From which it would be absurd to infer that the eagles there are not birds but a kind of quadruped.
